prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of the optical lattice clock

statement.case_for: The optical lattice clock is a clean idea, trapping neutral atoms at the magic wavelength so that the trap does not shift the clock transition, carried through to extraordinary quantitative control. Independent laboratories (Tokyo/RIKEN, JILA, SYRTE, PTB, NIST, NPL) have reproduced and surpassed one another's results over roughly two decades, and comparisons at the 1e-18 level are now routine. It has already produced new physics: millimetre-scale tests of the gravitational redshift, bounds on variation of constants, and searches for dark matter. It is also an unusually well-attributed discovery. Katori conceived the scheme and Ye's group drove the record accuracy and the many-body (Fermi-degenerate) clocks. All eight members ranked it, and five of eight placed it in the top six, which is not by itself merit but shows it is not a narrow taste of the atomic physicists. I rank it first because it is the combination of originality, reproducibility and a stable two-person attribution that I most trust.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is overlap. The 2005 prize (Hall and Haensch, the frequency comb) and the 2012 prize (Wineland and Haroche, trapped-ion control and ion clocks) lie close by, and some will say this is the next increment in optical metrology rather than a new discovery. The redefinition of the second has not yet happened, so the headline application is still prospective. There is also a legitimate attribution question about Lemonde, Gill, Ludlow, Hinkley and others who made decisive contributions to the clocks. I am a theorist in the same broad community, which is exactly why I want a colleague from outside AMO to test whether this reads as a fundamental result or as an instrument.

responses.point: Kroll ranks B040 first as a pure measurement advance: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength scheme, Ye built the best systems, and Hall/Haensch and Wineland already cover only adjacent ground, so the pair is the natural core.
responses.response: I agree on the pair and on maturity. I would put the case a little differently, though. The 2005 and 2012 prizes concerned how to measure frequency and how to control single ions. The lattice clock is a different thing, because it uses many neutral atoms at once, with the lattice light shift cancelled. That is why it opens many-body clock physics and Fermi-degenerate systems, and the ion-clock comparison does not capture it. Where I would push back is on B017, which we both rank second. Atom interferometry has a crowded and contested 1991 priority picture, with Chu and Mlynek outside the credited trio and Chu already a laureate. I like the physics, since it puts the quantum-classical boundary on the bench, but I do not think the attribution is clean enough to prefer it over B040.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks B061 first: topological insulators created a new class of quantum matter, and Kane and Mele plus Molenkamp form a theory-plus-experiment split, though credit for the HgTe proposal and the 3D generalisation sits outside the names.
responses.response: I accept that this is conceptually the larger shift. I ranked it fourth and I defer to you on the condensed-matter ranking. My reservation is about the credited names, not the physics. Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang proposed the HgTe quantum-well realisation that Molenkamp then measured, and Fu, Kane and Mele made the 3D generalisation. A prize to Kane, Mele and Molenkamp would leave out the proposal that the decisive experiment tested, and you list this yourself. The 2016 prize also covers the neighbouring topological concepts. If the committee can settle the HgTe credit question I would regard B061 as a serious second configuration, and I would like to hear from you whether Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang can be handled within three names. B040 does not have that problem.

responses.point: Pearce ranks IceCube first because it opened a new observational window, with Halzen driving the concept and Karle central to detector construction, while admitting that a collaboration of hundreds and earlier pioneers make credit hard.
responses.response: I share your value of opening a window, and the diffuse flux is firmly established. I ranked B018 sixth for two reasons. The first is attribution: Halzen and Karle are fair choices, but this is a discovery by a collaboration of hundreds, and DUMAND, AMANDA and the ice-calibration work are not credited. The second is that source-level conclusions (TXS 0506+056, NGC 1068, the Galactic plane) are still being consolidated, and the origin of most of the diffuse flux is open. I defer to you on astroparticle physics and I am prepared to be moved on maturity. Koshiba and Davis were honoured in 2002 for neutrino astronomy, so the committee should state explicitly why the 2013 detection is a new discovery rather than a continuation.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks B008 first, where Vicsek, Toner and Tu supply a minimal model and a hydrodynamic theory showing long-range order in a 2D active system, and ranks B040 fifth while still calling a two-person lattice-clock prize coherent.
responses.response: I find the Toner-Tu result elegant, and the evasion of the Mermin-Wagner intuition is the kind of thing I like to explain with a simple image. My doubt is the one you raise yourself. The experimental confirmation of the specific exponents is partial, and the qualitative flocking transition is clearer than the quantitative scaling. I take reproducibility seriously, and for the lattice clock it is overwhelming. Given that you consider the Katori and Ye attribution coherent, I would ask what in the metrology case holds your ranking at five. If it is the worry about another AMO prize so soon, I would like to examine it, since the 2022 prize concerned entanglement and Bell tests, which is not clock physics.

responses.point: Olsson ranks aberration-corrected electron microscopy first as a verified, widely used invention, but flags that Krivanek, who developed the STEM corrector, is not in the credited trio, and that the fit between instrumentation and discovery might be questioned.
responses.response: I agree that the correctors are in use everywhere and that the invention clause fits. We should be consistent, though, in how we treat instruments. I defend the lattice clock as a discovery-grade result, not only an instrument, because it has produced new measurements of the gravitational redshift and new bounds on constants. Your own flagged problem with Krivanek is a real one. If the committee insists on an even handed attribution for the TEM and STEM branches, three names may not suffice, and I would then rank B046 below B040. I do not hold that against the physics. It is a statement about which candidate is ready for a three-name citation.

uncertainties: How the committee weighs the lattice clock against the 2005 and 2012 prizes: new physics, or the next step in precision measurement.
Whether the pending redefinition of the second should be treated as confirmation or as evidence that the case is still prospective.
Credit to Lemonde, Gill, Ludlow, Hinkley and others outside Katori and Ye is unresolved, and I have not verified priority details between the Tokyo and JILA efforts.
Whether the HgTe credit question for B061 can be resolved within three names, and whether the overlap with the 2016 prize is decisive.
Whether the atom-interferometry priority picture for B017 (Borde, Pritchard, Kasevich, Chu, Mlynek) can be written fairly into a three-name citation.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict with B040 is apparent from my profile: I have no documented collaboration with Katori or Ye. I work in theoretical atomic physics at Stockholm University, and I am a long-time collaborator of Anne L'Huillier (2023 laureate), which is not a candidate here. I do know the broader AMO precision-measurement community, including Paul Indelicato and Reinhold Schuch, but none of them is on the shortlist. I flag that general closeness to the field and would accept scrutiny of my ranking of B040 and B017.
